intro: Mahler’s Fifth ends in D major with a horn tune, chasing string parts and a brass chorale big enough to fill the hall. Even the preceding Adagietto gets up and dances.

cues.title: One A becomes a conversation
cues.text: The horn holds an A, and the first violins hold it too, pp, dying away. Bassoon, oboe and clarinet try out little phrases around it, the oboe marked zögernd — hesitating. The finale begins as a conversation among a few players, each putting a tune on the table.
cues.evidence: Peters score (IMSLP #111956), p. 183: Allegro; first horn lang, verklingend; first violins pp lang, verklingend; bassoon f, oboe p zögernd, clarinet Etwas langsamer. Basinger’s Utah Symphony guide has the bassoon fragment sound only a few seconds into the movement: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/10/mahler-5-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The donkey judges the singers
cues.text: The bassoon’s little phrase comes from Mahler’s Wunderhorn song Lob des hohen Verstandes, “In praise of lofty intellect”. In the song a cuckoo and a nightingale hold a singing contest, and a donkey is the judge. He gives the prize to the cuckoo.
cues.evidence: Bettie Jo Basinger’s Utah Symphony guide names the bassoon fragment as derived from the setting of the Wunderhorn text Lob des hohen Verstands and prints the poem, in which the donkey awards the prize to the cuckoo: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/10/mahler-5-listening-guide/ . The bassoon phrase stands in the opening bars of Peters score (IMSLP #111956), p. 183.

cues.title: The horn finds a tune
cues.text: The horn gathers those small phrases into the rondo’s D-major tune, marked Allegro commodo, over a drone of open fifths in the bassoons. A second horn follows close behind. The folk-like melody will return like a refrain.
cues.evidence: Peters score (IMSLP #111956), p. 183: riten., Allegro commodo (Hauptzeitmass), D major, horns in imitation (the second horn’s entry marked 2.), sustained open fifths in the bassoons. Basinger: the folk-like giocoso theme is first played by the horn section over drone harmonies and recurs like a poetic refrain: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/10/mahler-5-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Cellos start the chase
cues.text: At rehearsal 2 Mahler writes Nicht eilen — don’t rush — and the cellos begin a running line. The basses and other strings enter behind them, p leggiero. This is a fugato: each new voice joins the conversation without silencing the others.
cues.evidence: Peters score (IMSLP #111956), pp. 185–186: rehearsal 2, Nicht eilen, cellos and basses with running eighths, then the successive string entries marked p leggiero. Basinger: fugal process is a chief level of organisation in the finale: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/10/mahler-5-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The Adagietto learns to dance
cues.text: The finale borrows a melody from the Adagietto and sets it among quick string figures. Its long, yearning phrases acquire a spring in their step: over the violins Mahler writes schwungvoll — with swing.
cues.evidence: Peters score (IMSLP #111956), p. 196 (rehearsal 8): first violins marked schwungvoll over quick string figures. Basinger: the Adagietto surfaces in the finale after the second refrain-fugue pair, transmuted into a grazioso, flowing dance: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/10/mahler-5-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Bach beside the lake
cues.text: While writing the Fifth, Mahler is also living with Bach’s collected works, to which he subscribes. The finale sends its string parts after one another in fugues and canons, then lets a horn stroll through with a tune.
cues.evidence: Mahler Foundation, Symphony No. 5 introduction, on the Bach edition and the finale’s contrapuntal writing. https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-5/symphony-no-5-introduction/

cues.title: A drop to two flats
cues.text: The music lurches from two sharps to two flats. Mahler writes Nicht eilen. (Pesante.) — don’t rush, weightily — and the running figure of the fugue re-enters in violas, cellos and basses beneath staccato horns and trombones.
cues.evidence: Peters score (IMSLP #111956), p. 224: two flats, Nicht eilen. (Pesante.), the running figure in violas, cellos and basses, staccato horns and trombones. Basinger: whenever the giocoso refrain recurs it precedes fugues on the wind motives of the introduction: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/10/mahler-5-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The chorale comes home
cues.text: The brass chorale returns in D major at Pesante (Etwas gehalten): horns, trumpets and trombones on broad fff chords with bells raised, a cymbal left to ring, quick strings running beneath. Earlier, the hymn dissolved back into the storm; here it carries on towards the symphony’s finish.
cues.evidence: Peters score (IMSLP #111956), p. 244: Pesante (Etwas gehalten), D major, brass fff, Schalltrichter auf, Becken klingen lassen, running string figures ff sempre. Basinger: a chorale reminiscent of the second movement materializes at the high point of the finale and a gradually accelerating coda brings the Fifth to a dramatic close: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/10/mahler-5-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A sharp last stroke
cues.text: The closing pages hurry into Presto: rushing chromatic runs in winds and strings, then short chords marked secco, with timpani, cymbals, bass drum and triangle told to damp quickly. The symphony ends on short, dry strokes.
cues.evidence: Peters score (IMSLP #111956), p. 251: Presto, chromatic runs, secco chords, schnell abdämpfen in the percussion, final bars. Basinger: the gradually accelerating coda brings the Fifth to a dramatic close: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/10/mahler-5-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Mahler plays the funeral march
cues.text: On 9 November 1905 Mahler sat at a Welte-Mignon reproducing piano in Leipzig and recorded the Fifth’s first movement, the funeral march, as a piano roll.
cues.evidence: The Mahler Foundation’s history page for the symphony lists the 1905 Leipzig recording of Movement 1: Trauermarsch (piano): https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-5/symphony-no-5-history/

transitions.title: The oboe hands over to the horn
transitions.from: Intro · Horn, bassoon, oboe and clarinet
transitions.to: A · Horn tune and chasing strings
transitions.how: After a riten. the horn takes the main tune at Allegro commodo (Hauptzeitmass), with a second horn following in imitation. Open fifths in the bassoons hold D major beneath the tune’s falling phrases.
transitions.evidence: Peters score (IMSLP #111956), p. 183: riten., Allegro commodo (Hauptzeitmass), horns in imitation, open fifths in the bassoons. Basinger: the giocoso theme is first played by the horn section over drone harmonies.

transitions.title: The brass open into D major
transitions.to: Coda · Brass chorale and final rush
transitions.how: Horns, trumpets and trombones swell to a broad D-major chord at Pesante (Etwas gehalten), with bells raised and a cymbal left to ring. The strings keep their quick figures moving underneath, carrying the hymn into the faster coda.
transitions.evidence: Peters score (IMSLP #111956), p. 244: Pesante (Etwas gehalten), brass crescendo to fff, Schalltrichter auf, Becken klingen lassen, running strings. Basinger: a chorale reminiscent of the second movement materializes at the high point.

source.title: Mahler, Symphony No. 5, V, Peters study score, plate 9015
source.locator: Printed p. 183: horn and woodwind introduction; pp. 185–186: string fugato; p. 210: horn and string melody; pp. 244–251: brass chorale and closing pages.

timeline.note: A horn note sets off short replies from bassoon, oboe and clarinet.
The horn carries the rondo tune above woodwinds and low strings.
Cellos start the fugato; other string sections take up the running line.
Horn and strings sing longer phrases above held woodwind notes.
The brass chorale rises above running strings and the full orchestra.
Fast orchestral figures rush towards the short closing chords.
The written finale closes in D major.

composer.epithet: A conductor who composed in the summers, and wanted each symphony to hold a whole world — the sublime and the street band together.
facts: Vienna Conservatory, 1875–78: piano with Julius Epstein, composition with Franz Krenn; attended Bruckner’s university lectures
Budapest Royal Opera 1888–91 · Hamburg Stadttheater 1891–97 · Vienna Court Opera 1897–1907 · Metropolitan Opera and New York Philharmonic 1908–11
In summer huts at Steinbach am Attersee, Maiernigg on the Wörthersee, and Toblach in the Dolomites
Nine numbered symphonies and an unfinished Tenth; Das Lied von der Erde; orchestral songs

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. Iglau gave him the sounds that never left his music: bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church. A story he told late in life, to Sigmund Freud, describes running from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was grinding out Ach, du lieber Augustin. Tragedy and the banal, side by side: it is a fair description of half his slow movements.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, studying piano and composition, and sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. His friends were Hugo Wolf and the short-lived Hans Rott, whose symphony sounds so much like Mahler’s own that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony, as he understood it. The cantata Das klagende Lied, completed in 1880, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881. He had already begun the career that would pay for everything else: conducting.
